text: A UI Test is the most literal application of the Test Step idea from Lesson 12. It's a sequence of reusable Test Steps that simulate a real person clicking through the actual ServiceNow interface, in the exact order a real user would, with ServiceNow logging exactly what happened at each step.

A typical UI Test strings together four kinds of steps: open a specific form, set a field's value the way a user would type into it, submit the form — the equivalent of clicking Save — and then verify the result, confirming something specific is now true.

That verification step is what separates a real UI Test from blindly clicking through. A Test that only opens and submits a form proves it didn't error — it proves nothing about whether the right thing happened. Checking a specific, concrete outcome is what actually catches a logic regression.

One of ATF's most important real capabilities is the Impersonate User step. Without it, every UI Test runs as whichever account launched it — almost always an administrator, who can see every field and bypass most restrictions.

Course 3 and Course 6 both showed that UI Policies can hide or restrict a field based on the current user's role, and an admin account often never triggers that condition at all. Impersonate User makes the Test run as a specific real user and role, so the same UI Policies, field-level ACLs, and visibility rules apply during the Test.

A UI Test is slower to build than a server-side Test, because it has to account for page load timing and which fields are even visible to the impersonated role. That cost buys something a server-side Test can't: confirmation that the actual end-user experience works, not just the logic underneath it.
